chunks: Ali from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr and Safwan from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
When you enter the state of Ihram, avoid killing all animals, except the viper, the scorpion, and the rat, for they damage the water skins and burn down the houses of the people.

And as for the scorpion, the Prophet of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) extended his hand to the stone, and a scorpion stung him, so he said: 'May Allah curse you! You do not spare the righteous nor the sinner.'
And the snake, if it intends (to attack) you, kill it; if it does not intend (to attack) you, do not intend (to attack) it.
And the vicious dog and the wild beast, if they intend (to attack) you, kill them; if they do not intend (to attack) you, do not intend (to attack) them.
And the treacherous black snake, kill it in all cases, and throw the crow and the buzzard upon the back of your camel.

key_terms.إِحْرَامٌ: The state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What animals can a pilgrim in Ihram kill and which must they spare according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) via the reliable chain of Safwan and Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar, establishes the principle of 'takhalluf' (removal of pests) during Hajj, balancing ritual purity with practical necessity. It distinguishes between 'muhibb al-bayt' (pests that damage property, like rats) which are always permissible to kill, and 'muharrif' (animals that attack, like snakes) where killing is conditional on their aggression, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on intent and harm. The inclusion of specific birds like the crow and kite highlights the detailed application of these rules to both terrestrial and aerial threats during the sacred state.
